nuance.usage_note: Patristic writers adapted a three-part model of the soul: the rational (logistikon), the incensive or irascible (thymikon) and the desiring power (epithymetikon). Ascetic life does not destroy desire but redirects it, so that it becomes longing for God, or divine eros. The Philokalia translators often render it "desiring power" or "appetitive aspect."

distinctions.note: The incensive power (thymikon) is the soul's energy of anger and zeal; the desiring power is its longing.
Lust is the desiring power misdirected; the power itself is good.
The will is the faculty of choice; the desiring power is the appetite that the will can guide.

collocations: the desiring power of the soul

examples.everyday: Father said the problem isn't that we want too much, it's that our desiring power is pointed at the wrong things.
examples.professional: Explain the desiring power with the tripartite soul before introducing the eight logismoi.
examples.analytical: For Maximus, the desiring power is fulfilled when it is transformed into an insatiable longing for God.

nuance.analogy: Like a river that floods when it overflows its banks but waters a whole valley when channeled.
nuance.etymology: Translates Greek epithymetikon, from epithymia, "desire."
common_mistakes: Thinking ascetics want to destroy desire.
Confusing it with sexual desire alone.

senses: A fifth-century Greek bishop of Photike in Epirus whose One Hundred Texts on spiritual knowledge and discernment appear in the Philokalia.

etymology: Greek Diadochos, "successor"; Photike, a city in Epirus, northwestern Greece.

core.definition: A fifth-century Greek bishop of Photike in Epirus whose One Hundred Texts on spiritual knowledge and discernment appear in the Philokalia.

pronunciation.tip: Americans usually say "dy-AD-uh-kus"; Greek speakers say "dee-AH-tho-hos." Also spelled Diadochus of Photice ("FOH-tih-see").

nuance.usage_note: Diadochos is valued for teaching on the "spiritual sense" of the soul, the discernment of spirits, and remembrance of the Lord Jesus, which anticipates the Jesus Prayer. He opposed the Messalian idea that grace and sin coexist equally in the baptized. He is read in courses on the Philokalia and early Byzantine spirituality.

distinctions.note: Dorotheos writes practical counsel for monks; Diadochos writes more on spiritual perception and grace.
Evagrius is more speculative; Diadochos balances him with the language of the heart and experience.
The Macarian homilies stress the heart and experience like Diadochos, but Diadochos rejects Messalian views of sin and grace.

collocations: Diadochos of Photiki's One Hundred Texts

examples.everyday: Our reading group started the Philokalia with Diadochos of Photiki; his chapters on discernment are so clear.
examples.professional: In the syllabus, Diadochos of Photiki bridges Evagrius and the later hesychasts.
examples.analytical: Diadochos of Photiki's teaching that grace dwells in the depth of the baptized soul is a corrective to Messalian anthropology.

nuance.etymology: Greek Diadochos, "successor"; Photike, a city in Epirus, northwestern Greece.
common_mistakes: Mispronouncing Photiki with an f-o-t-i-k-eye ending.
Placing him in the fourteenth century with the hesychasts.

senses: A monastic's assigned work or task in the monastery, also called an obedience, done as service to God and the community.

etymology: Greek diakonema, "service, task," from diakonein, "to serve."

core.definition: A monastic's assigned work or task in the monastery, also called an obedience, done as service to God and the community.

pronunciation.tip: Stress KOH. Greek speakers say "dee-ah-KOH-nee-mah"; the plural is diakonimata.

nuance.usage_note: Used in English-speaking Orthodox monasteries, especially those connected with Mount Athos and Greek monasticism; Russian-tradition communities usually say "obedience" (poslushanie). Examples are cooking, gardening, guest master, or icon painting. The work is received from the abbot, not chosen for oneself.

distinctions.note: Obedience is the English (and Russian) term for the same assignment; diakonima is the Greek.
Diakonia is service or ministry in general; diakonima is a specific monastic task.
A job is chosen and paid; a diakonima is given by the abbot as part of the spiritual life.

examples.everyday: Sister Maria's diakonima is the candle workshop, so she always smells of beeswax.
examples.professional: The abbot assigns each novice a diakonima to test humility and patience.
examples.analytical: The diakonima turns manual labor into liturgy: work done in obedience becomes prayer.

nuance.etymology: Greek diakonema, "service, task," from diakonein, "to serve."
common_mistakes: Using it for a paid parish job.
Treating it as a hobby: it is not chosen by the monk.

senses: Discernment: the spiritual gift and virtue of distinguishing good from evil, true thoughts from deceptive ones, and the right measure in every action.

etymology: Greek diakrisis, "distinguishing, judging," from diakrinein, "to separate, discern."

core.definition: Discernment: the spiritual gift and virtue of distinguishing good from evil, true thoughts from deceptive ones, and the right measure in every action.

pronunciation.tip: Stress AH. Some Americans say "dy-AK-rih-sis"; Greek speakers say "dee-AH-kree-sees."

nuance.usage_note: In the desert tradition discernment is called the greatest or royal virtue, because without it even fasting and prayer can lead to pride or ruin; John Cassian records Antony teaching this. It covers discerning thoughts, discerning spirits, and moderation. Most English writers simply say "discernment"; diakrisis appears in academic and Orthodox writing.

distinctions.note: Discretion is Cassian's Latin rendering (discretio), stressing moderation; diakrisis also means discerning spirits.
Judgment can mean condemning others; diakrisis is spiritual insight, not criticism.
Prudence is the practical virtue of wise choice; diakrisis is a grace-given perception of spiritual realities.

examples.everyday: When I asked about fasting stricter, Father said, "Diakrisis first," and told me to do less.
examples.professional: Spiritual fathers need diakrisis to know when to be strict and when to be gentle.
examples.analytical: Diakrisis governs all other virtues: it measures fasting, vigil and silence so that they serve love.

nuance.analogy: Like a ship's navigator: without him, even a strong crew can sail onto the rocks.
nuance.etymology: Greek diakrisis, "distinguishing, judging," from diakrinein, "to separate, discern."
common_mistakes: Confusing it with "diagnosis."
Using it to mean criticizing others.
nuance.biblical_note: In 1 Corinthians 12:10 Paul lists "the ability to distinguish between spirits" (diakriseis pneumaton) among the gifts of the Spirit. Hebrews 5:14 speaks of the mature whose faculties are trained by practice to distinguish good from evil. 1 John 4:1 urges believers to test the spirits.

senses: Paul's Athenian convert (Acts 17:34), and the name used by an anonymous writer around 500 whose works shaped Christian mystical and liturgical theology.

etymology: Areopagite, "member of the Areopagus," the council of Athens that met on the hill of Ares.

core.definition: Paul's Athenian convert (Acts 17:34), and the name used by an anonymous writer around 500 whose works shaped Christian mystical and liturgical theology.

pronunciation.tip: Stress NISH and AH. "Areopagite" ends with a hard g, "-gyte"; some say "-jyte." Scholars call the author Pseudo-Dionysius.

nuance.connotation: Positive; scholars debate how the pseudonym should affect his authority.
nuance.usage_note: The writings include The Divine Names, The Mystical Theology, The Celestial Hierarchy, The Ecclesiastical Hierarchy and ten letters. They introduced apophatic theology, the nine ranks of angels and a symbolic reading of the liturgy. Maximus the Confessor and Gregory Palamas read him in an Orthodox sense; in the West he deeply influenced Thomas Aquinas and medieval mystics.

distinctions.note: A third-century bishop of Alexandria, a different person.
Pseudo-Dionysius is the scholarly name for the author c. 500; Dionysius the Areopagite properly names Paul's convert.
Dionysus is the Greek god of wine; Dionysius is a Christian name derived from it.

collocations: the writings of Dionysius the Areopagite

examples.everyday: Our reading group is starting Dionysius the Areopagite next month; I hear the Mystical Theology is short but hard.
examples.professional: Any survey of Byzantine liturgical commentary must begin with Dionysius the Areopagite's Ecclesiastical Hierarchy.
examples.analytical: Dionysius the Areopagite's apophaticism does not abolish affirmation but surpasses it through negation.

nuance.etymology: Areopagite, "member of the Areopagus," the council of Athens that met on the hill of Ares.
common_mistakes: Confusing Dionysius with the god Dionysus.
Assuming all scholars accept his first-century authorship: modern scholarship dates the writings around 500.
nuance.biblical_note: Acts 17:34 names Dionysius the Areopagite among those in Athens who joined Paul and believed after his speech at the Areopagus (Acts 17:22-31), in which Paul proclaims the "unknown god."

senses: The mystical experience of God as beyond all knowledge, where the soul meets God by going past concepts; also called the darkness of unknowing.

etymology: Translates Greek theios gnophos; gnophos is the word for the darkness on Sinai in the Greek Old Testament.

core.definition: The mystical experience of God as beyond all knowledge, where the soul meets God by going past concepts; also called the darkness of unknowing.

pronunciation.tip: Stress VYN and DAHRK. The first syllable of "divine" is a weak "dih."

nuance.connotation: Positive; paradoxical, meaning brightness too great for the mind.
nuance.usage_note: Gregory of Nyssa, in the Life of Moses, describes Moses' ascent from light into darkness as growth in knowing God. Dionysius the Areopagite speaks of the "ray of divine darkness" in the Mystical Theology. The phrase is common in theology and spirituality, never meaning evil.

distinctions.note: John of the Cross's dark night is a painful purification; divine darkness is God's own unknowability.
The English medieval phrase for a related idea.
Divine light is God's uncreated glory seen by the saints; Palamas holds that divine darkness and divine light describe the same reality.

examples.everyday: Our priest said that when prayer feels dark, it might be the divine darkness, God being bigger than our ideas.
examples.professional: This chapter traces divine darkness from Philo through Gregory of Nyssa to Dionysius.
examples.analytical: In the divine darkness, unknowing is not ignorance but the highest form of knowledge, a knowing above knowing.

nuance.analogy: Like looking at the sun: the brighter it is, the less you see.
nuance.etymology: Translates Greek theios gnophos; gnophos is the word for the darkness on Sinai in the Greek Old Testament.
common_mistakes: Reading it as evil or demonic darkness.
Confusing it with depression or spiritual dryness.
nuance.biblical_note: Exodus 20:21 says Moses drew near to the thick darkness where God was. Psalm 18:11 says God made darkness his covering. 1 Timothy 6:16 says God dwells in unapproachable light, which the Fathers paired with the darkness texts.

senses: God's ecstatic, self-giving love for creation, and the soul's passionate longing for God in response.

etymology: Greek eros, "love, desire"; adopted for God by Dionysius the Areopagite.

core.definition: God's ecstatic, self-giving love for creation, and the soul's passionate longing for God in response.

pronunciation.tip: Stress VYN and AIR. Americans say "eros" as "AIR-ahs" or "EER-ahs."

nuance.connotation: Positive; in modern English "erotic" suggests sex, so the term can surprise.
nuance.usage_note: Dionysius the Areopagite, in The Divine Names, defends calling God's love eros and says it is ecstatic: it takes God "out of himself" toward creation. He cites Ignatius of Antioch's words "my eros has been crucified." Maximus the Confessor develops the idea. Used in theology classes; explain it, since listeners may hear only the sexual meaning.

distinctions.note: Agape is self-giving love; divine eros adds passionate longing and desire, and the Fathers treated them as one.
Everyday eros means sexual desire; divine eros is love's longing purified and directed to God.
Charity is love expressed in action; divine eros names the burning love behind it.

examples.everyday: I was surprised when Father talked about divine eros, but he meant God's longing love for us.
examples.professional: Before reading Dionysius, students should know why he prefers eros to agape for God's love.
examples.analytical: Divine eros is ecstatic: it draws the lover out of self toward the beloved, as God goes out to creation.

nuance.analogy: Like a bridegroom who cannot stay away from his bride.
nuance.etymology: Greek eros, "love, desire"; adopted for God by Dionysius the Areopagite.
common_mistakes: Translating it as "divine sexuality."
Pronouncing eros as "ee-ROSE."
nuance.biblical_note: The Song of Songs, read by the Fathers as the love of God and the soul, is the main biblical basis. Hosea 2:14-20 depicts God wooing Israel as a bride. The Greek word eros itself is rare in the Bible; the New Testament uses agape.

senses: The uncreated light of God's glory, seen by the apostles at the Transfiguration and by saints in prayer; also called the Taboric light.

etymology: Divine from Latin divinus; light from Old English leoht.

core.definition: The uncreated light of God's glory, seen by the apostles at the Transfiguration and by saints in prayer; also called the Taboric light.

pronunciation.tip: Stress VYN and LYT. Final t is often unreleased in American speech.

nuance.usage_note: In Orthodox theology the divine light is not a created symbol but God's own energy, as Gregory Palamas defended in the fourteenth century. Symeon the New Theologian wrote of seeing it. In general Christian usage the phrase can simply mean God's guidance or truth.

distinctions.note: Uncreated light is the technical Palamite term; divine light is broader.
The Taboric light is the divine light as seen on Mount Tabor.
Illumination is the stage of the spiritual life or the gift of enlightenment; divine light is what is seen.

examples.everyday: At Transfiguration, Father said the disciples saw the divine light that the saints still see in prayer.
examples.professional: The hesychast controversy turned on whether the divine light is created or uncreated.
examples.analytical: For Palamas, the divine light is God himself in his energies, not the essence, yet truly God.

nuance.analogy: Like sunlight that is truly the sun reaching you, though not the sun's core.
nuance.etymology: Divine from Latin divinus; light from Old English leoht.
common_mistakes: Assuming it is a mere metaphor in Orthodox teaching.
Writing "devine."
nuance.biblical_note: Matthew 17:2 says Jesus' face shone like the sun at the Transfiguration. Psalm 36:9 says "in thy light do we see light." 1 John 1:5 says God is light, and in him there is no darkness.

senses: What God is: the one nature shared by Father, Son and Holy Spirit; in Christ, His divinity alongside His human nature.

etymology: Latin natura divina; translates Greek theia physis.

core.definition: What God is: the one nature shared by Father, Son and Holy Spirit; in Christ, His divinity alongside His human nature.

pronunciation.tip: Stress VYN and NAY. The t in "nature" sounds like ch.

nuance.usage_note: Used in Trinitarian theology (one nature or essence, three persons) and Christology (Chalcedon's two natures in one person). In Orthodox theology the divine nature is unknowable and unshareable in its essence, so "partaking of the divine nature" (2 Peter 1:4) is explained as participation in God's energies.

distinctions.note: Essence (ousia) is close in meaning; theologians often use nature and essence interchangeably for God.
A person (hypostasis) is who; nature is what. God is three persons in one nature.
The energies are God's activity, in which creatures can share; the nature in itself remains beyond them.

collocations: one divine nature in three persons

examples.everyday: In Bible study we read that we can be partakers of the divine nature, and everyone wanted to know what that means.
examples.professional: Teaching on Chalcedon should clarify that Christ's divine nature is not mixed with his human nature.
examples.analytical: The Cappadocians argued that the divine nature is common to the three hypostases while remaining incomprehensible.

nuance.etymology: Latin natura divina; translates Greek theia physis.
common_mistakes: Confusing nature (what) with person (who).
Writing "devine nature."
nuance.biblical_note: 2 Peter 1:4 promises that believers may become partakers of the divine nature (theias koinonoi physeos). Romans 1:20 speaks of God's eternal power and deity seen in creation. Colossians 2:9 says the whole fullness of deity dwells bodily in Christ.

senses: The Slavonic and Russian translation of the Philokalia, first published by Paisius Velichkovsky in 1793 and later expanded in Russian by Theophan the Recluse.

etymology: Slavonic dobrotoliubie, "love of the good," calque of Greek philokalia, "love of the beautiful."

core.definition: The Slavonic and Russian translation of the Philokalia, first published by Paisius Velichkovsky in 1793 and later expanded in Russian by Theophan the Recluse.

pronunciation.tip: Stress LYOO. Russian unstressed o's sound like "uh." Also spelled Dobrotolubie.

nuance.usage_note: The Dobrotolubiye brought hesychast teaching to Russia and fed the nineteenth-century revival of eldership at Optina. The pilgrim in The Way of a Pilgrim carries it with him. Theophan the Recluse's Russian version, in five volumes, was much expanded. English speakers usually say "the Russian Philokalia."

distinctions.note: The Philokalia is the Greek collection of 1782; the Dobrotolubiye is its Slavonic and Russian version.
The Way of a Pilgrim is a narrative about the Jesus Prayer that cites the Dobrotolubiye.
Optina is the monastery where the Dobrotolubiye's teaching flourished.

examples.everyday: In The Way of a Pilgrim, the pilgrim reads the Dobrotolubiye and learns how to pray the Jesus Prayer.
examples.professional: Graduate students should compare the Greek Philokalia with the Dobrotolubiye's selections.
examples.analytical: The Dobrotolubiye transformed Russian monasticism by making hesychast sources available in Slavonic.

nuance.etymology: Slavonic dobrotoliubie, "love of the good," calque of Greek philokalia, "love of the beautiful."
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable.
Thinking it is identical to the Greek Philokalia.

senses: The two-week Orthodox fast from August 1 to 14 that prepares for the feast of the Dormition of the Theotokos on August 15.

etymology: Dormition from Latin dormitio, "falling asleep"; fast from Old English faestan.

core.definition: The two-week Orthodox fast from August 1 to 14 that prepares for the feast of the Dormition of the Theotokos on August 15.

pronunciation.tip: Stress MISH and FAST. Americans say "fast" with the short a of "cat."

nuance.usage_note: One of the four fasting seasons of the Orthodox year, with Great Lent, the Apostles' Fast and the Nativity Fast. It is fairly strict, like Lent, but fish is allowed on the Transfiguration (August 6). Many parishes serve the Paraklesis to the Theotokos on its evenings.

distinctions.note: Great Lent precedes Pascha and lasts about seven weeks; the Dormition Fast is two weeks.
The Nativity Fast, before Christmas, is forty days and less strict.
The Apostles' Fast, before June 29, varies in length with the date of Pascha.

collocations: the Paraklesis in the Dormition Fast

examples.everyday: We're in the Dormition Fast, so I'll bring a bean salad to the neighbors' barbecue instead of burgers.
examples.professional: Parish calendars should list the Paraklesis services held during the Dormition Fast.
examples.analytical: The Dormition Fast frames Mary's death within the Church's pattern of fasting before feasting.

nuance.etymology: Dormition from Latin dormitio, "falling asleep"; fast from Old English faestan.
common_mistakes: Thinking it is about Mary fasting.
Assuming it lasts forty days.

senses: A sixth-century monk near Gaza, disciple of Barsanuphius and John, whose Discourses teach humility, self-reproach and cutting off the will.

etymology: Greek Dorotheos, "gift of God"; Gaza, a city in Palestine.

core.definition: A sixth-century monk near Gaza, disciple of Barsanuphius and John, whose Discourses teach humility, self-reproach and cutting off the will.

pronunciation.tip: Stress THEE and GAH. Also spelled Dorotheus. The th is soft as in "think."

nuance.usage_note: His Discourses (Instructions) are among the most read monastic texts in Orthodox monasteries, and were translated into Latin and widely used in the West too. He is famous for the image of a circle: the closer we come to God at the center, the closer we come to one another. He is also a model of gentle spiritual direction.

distinctions.note: Barsanuphius was his elder; Dorotheos is the disciple who wrote the Discourses.
Climacus writes the Ladder at Sinai; Dorotheos's Discourses are simpler and more conversational.
Diadochos focuses on spiritual perception; Dorotheos on practical humility.

examples.everyday: Our study group loved Abba Dorotheos's circle diagram; it made love of God and neighbor so clear.
examples.professional: Many abbots give novices Dorotheos of Gaza as their first reading.
examples.analytical: Dorotheos of Gaza's teaching on self-reproach locates the root of every conflict in self-justification.

nuance.etymology: Greek Dorotheos, "gift of God"; Gaza, a city in Palestine.
common_mistakes: Confusing him with Dorotheus of Tyre.
Stressing the first syllable of Dorotheos.

senses: The Orthodox view that mystical union with God is lived within the Church, through sacraments, Scripture and Tradition, not as private experience.

etymology: Ecclesial from Greek ekklesia, "assembly, church"; mysticism from Greek mystikos, "secret."

core.definition: The Orthodox view that mystical union with God is lived within the Church, through sacraments, Scripture and Tradition, not as private experience.

pronunciation.tip: Stress KLEE and MIS. "Ecclesial" begins with a weak "ih."

nuance.usage_note: Associated especially with Vladimir Lossky, whose Mystical Theology of the Eastern Church argued that theology and mysticism are inseparable within the Church. Nicholas Cabasilas's The Life in Christ grounds mystical life in baptism, chrismation and the Eucharist. Used in academic theology to contrast with individualistic or psychological approaches to mysticism.

distinctions.note: Mystical theology is the knowledge of God in union; ecclesial mysticism stresses its setting in the Church.
Private revelation is a vision given to an individual; ecclesial mysticism is communal and sacramental.
Sacramental theology studies the sacraments; ecclesial mysticism describes the union with God they give.

examples.everyday: Father said our mysticism is ecclesial mysticism; we grow closer to God through the Liturgy, not alone in our rooms.
examples.professional: This course defends ecclesial mysticism against purely experiential models of mysticism.
examples.analytical: Ecclesial mysticism denies any opposition between the hierarchy and the charismatic life of the saints.

nuance.etymology: Ecclesial from Greek ekklesia, "assembly, church"; mysticism from Greek mystikos, "secret."
common_mistakes: Confusing "ecclesial" with "ecclesiastical."
Thinking it rejects personal experience.

senses: The theology that the Church is fully realized in each local Eucharistic assembly gathered around its bishop.

etymology: Coined in the twentieth century; from Eucharist + ecclesiology.

core.definition: The theology that the Church is fully realized in each local Eucharistic assembly gathered around its bishop.

pronunciation.tip: Stress RIS and AH. Say "ecclesiology" in five beats: ih-klee-zee-AH-luh-jee.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive; debated among theologians.
nuance.usage_note: Developed by Nicholas Afanasiev (The Church of the Holy Spirit) and corrected by John Zizioulas, who stressed the bishop and the communion of local churches. It influenced Vatican II's theology of the local church. Critics argue that it can neglect the universal Church or mission beyond the liturgy.

distinctions.note: A broader framework; Eucharistic ecclesiology focuses on the Eucharist as constituting the Church.
Universal ecclesiology starts with the Church worldwide; Eucharistic ecclesiology with the local Eucharist.
Sacramental theology studies the sacraments; Eucharistic ecclesiology is about what the Church is.

examples.everyday: My professor says Eucharistic ecclesiology changed how many Orthodox priests think about the parish.
examples.professional: This dissertation compares Afanasiev's and Zizioulas's forms of Eucharistic ecclesiology.
examples.analytical: Eucharistic ecclesiology locates catholicity not in size but in the fullness of the local Eucharist.

nuance.etymology: Coined in the twentieth century; from Eucharist + ecclesiology.
common_mistakes: Confusing ecclesiology with ecclesiastical history.
Thinking it means the Eucharist is only a symbol of unity.

senses: Evagrius's list of eight principal evil thoughts: gluttony, lust, greed, sadness, anger, acedia, vainglory and pride.

etymology: Greek logismoi, "thoughts, reasonings," from logos.

core.definition: Evagrius's list of eight principal evil thoughts: gluttony, lust, greed, sadness, anger, acedia, vainglory and pride.

pronunciation.tip: Americans usually say "lah-giz-MOY"; Greek speakers say "lo-yee-ZMEE." The singular is logismos.

nuance.usage_note: Evagrius of Pontus set out the list in the fourth century; John Cassian brought it to the West, and Gregory the Great later reshaped it into the seven deadly sins. The logismoi are not just ideas but tempting thought-patterns that feed passions. Used in courses on monasticism and in Orthodox spiritual direction.

distinctions.note: The seven deadly sins are the later Western list; the eight logismoi are its Eastern ancestor.
Passions are settled diseases of the soul; logismoi are the thoughts that lead to them.
The eight passions is Cassian's term for nearly the same list.

examples.everyday: Our Lent study is on the eight logismoi; I recognized acedia right away.
examples.professional: Students will compare the eight logismoi with Gregory the Great's seven deadly sins.
examples.analytical: Evagrius's eight logismoi function as a diagnostic map for the therapy of the soul.

nuance.analogy: Like a doctor's list of common infections, so the patient can name the sickness.
nuance.etymology: Greek logismoi, "thoughts, reasonings," from logos.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing logismoi like "logic."
Thinking a logismos is just any thought.

senses: John Cassian's eight principal vices: gluttony, lust, avarice, anger, sadness, acedia, vainglory and pride; ancestor of the seven deadly sins.

etymology: Passion from Latin passio, "suffering," translating Greek pathos.

core.definition: John Cassian's eight principal vices: gluttony, lust, avarice, anger, sadness, acedia, vainglory and pride; ancestor of the seven deadly sins.

pronunciation.tip: Stress AYT and PASH. "Passions" has a short a, as in "cat."

nuance.usage_note: Cassian, writing in Latin, transmitted the Evagrian list to the West in his Institutes and Conferences, with anger before sadness. In Orthodox spiritual writing "the eight passions" is a common teaching tool. Gregory the Great reduced the list to seven, merging vainglory with pride and adding envy.

distinctions.note: The eight logismoi are the thoughts; the eight passions are the disordered states they produce.
The later Western list of seven, shaped by Gregory the Great.
Passions in this sense are not emotions but spiritual diseases.

examples.everyday: Father gave a talk on the eight passions and said gluttony is the first because it's the easiest door.
examples.professional: Lecture notes should show how the eight passions map onto the seven deadly sins.
examples.analytical: Cassian's ordering of the eight passions suggests a causal chain, from bodily to spiritual vices.

nuance.etymology: Passion from Latin passio, "suffering," translating Greek pathos.
common_mistakes: Using "passion" in its modern positive sense ("my passion for music").
Saying there are seven passions in the Eastern tradition.

senses: The eight root vices named by Evagrius and Cassian: gluttony, lust, avarice, sadness, anger, acedia, vainglory and pride.

etymology: Principal from Latin principalis, "first, chief"; vice from Latin vitium, "fault."

core.definition: The eight root vices named by Evagrius and Cassian: gluttony, lust, avarice, sadness, anger, acedia, vainglory and pride.

pronunciation.tip: Stress AYT, PRIN and VY. "Principal" sounds just like "principle."

nuance.usage_note: This is the more neutral, scholarly English name for the Evagrian-Cassianic list. It is common in monastic history and spiritual theology, especially when comparing it with the seven deadly sins.

distinctions.note: The later Western list of seven.
The Greek name for the same list, seen as thoughts.
Mortal sins are a Catholic moral category; the principal vices are dispositions.

collocations: the doctrine of the eight principal vices
remedies for the eight principal vices

examples.everyday: Our reading group finished Cassian's chapters on the eight principal vices.
examples.professional: The eight principal vices form the structure of Books 5 to 12 of Cassian's Institutes.
examples.analytical: The eight principal vices function less as a moral code than as a diagnosis of the soul's illnesses.

nuance.etymology: Principal from Latin principalis, "first, chief"; vice from Latin vitium, "fault."
common_mistakes: Writing "principle vices."
Treating vices as single acts rather than habits.

senses: Greek for "energy" or "activity": in Orthodox theology, God's uncreated operations, through which He is truly present and known.

etymology: Greek energeia, "activity, operation," from ergon, "work."

core.definition: Greek for "energy" or "activity": in Orthodox theology, God's uncreated operations, through which He is truly present and known.

pronunciation.tip: Stress NER. American scholars say "eh-NER-gay-uh"; Greek speakers say "eh-NEHR-yee-ah."

nuance.usage_note: Aristotle used energeia for actuality; the Fathers applied it to God's acts. Gregory Palamas taught that God's energeia is uncreated and distinct from His essence (ousia), yet inseparable. Used in Byzantine theology and philosophy classes; ordinary speakers say "energies."

distinctions.note: Dynamis is power or potential; energeia is actuality or activity.
Ousia is essence; energeia is God's activity outside that essence.
Grace is God's gift; the Orthodox identify it with God's uncreated energeia.

examples.everyday: In theology class we learned that energeia isn't like electricity; it's God's activity.
examples.professional: Students should trace energeia from Aristotle to Palamas.
examples.analytical: Energeia allows Orthodox theology to affirm real participation in God without collapsing creature into Creator.

nuance.etymology: Greek energeia, "activity, operation," from ergon, "work."
common_mistakes: Using it to mean physical energy.
Pronouncing it "en-er-JEE-uh."

senses: In Orthodox theology, God's uncreated activities and powers, through which He acts and makes Himself known, distinct from His unknowable essence.

etymology: From Greek energeia, "activity."

core.definition: In Orthodox theology, God's uncreated activities and powers, through which He acts and makes Himself known, distinct from His unknowable essence.

pronunciation.tip: Stress EN. The g sounds like j.

nuance.usage_note: Gregory Palamas defended the doctrine of the divine energies in the fourteenth century; councils in Constantinople endorsed it. Orthodox theologians use the term to explain theosis, the light of Tabor and grace. In everyday English, "energies" means physical or emotional vigor.

distinctions.note: The essence is what God is in Himself; the energies are God acting.
Grace is God's gift; in Orthodoxy grace is an uncreated energy.
In Western theology, attributes are qualities of God's simple being; the energies are really distinct from the essence.

examples.everyday: Father explained that we can't know God's essence, but we meet Him in His energies.
examples.professional: Palamas's teaching on the energies is a central topic in Orthodox dogmatics.
examples.analytical: The energies preserve both apophaticism and real communion with God.

nuance.etymology: From Greek energeia, "activity."
common_mistakes: Assuming it is New Age language.
Thinking the energies are created things.

senses: Gregory of Nyssa's teaching that the soul eternally stretches forward into God, growing without end because God is infinite.

etymology: Greek epektasis, "stretching out," from epekteinesthai, "to strain forward."

core.definition: Gregory of Nyssa's teaching that the soul eternally stretches forward into God, growing without end because God is infinite.

pronunciation.tip: Stress PEK. Greek speakers say "eh-PEK-tah-sees."

nuance.usage_note: Gregory develops it in the Life of Moses and the Homilies on the Song of Songs: perfection is endless progress. The term comes from Paul's "straining forward." Used in patristic and spiritual theology.

distinctions.note: Theosis is union with God; epektasis describes its endless growth.
Ordinary progress has an end; epektasis does not.
The beatific vision is the final sight of God; epektasis stresses never-ending ascent.

examples.everyday: Father said heaven won't be boring; Gregory of Nyssa called it epektasis, always going deeper.
examples.professional: Seminar participants will trace epektasis through the Life of Moses.
examples.analytical: Epektasis redefines perfection as unending growth.

nuance.etymology: Greek epektasis, "stretching out," from epekteinesthai, "to strain forward."
common_mistakes: Confusing it with "ectasis" or "ecstasy."
Thinking it implies imperfection in heaven.
nuance.biblical_note: Philippians 3:13-14, where Paul forgets what lies behind and strains forward (epekteinomenos) to what lies ahead, is the source of the term.

senses: The Orthodox teaching that God's essence is unknowable and unshareable, while His uncreated energies are truly God and can be shared.

etymology: Essence from Latin essentia (Greek ousia); energies from Greek energeia.

core.definition: The Orthodox teaching that God's essence is unknowable and unshareable, while His uncreated energies are truly God and can be shared.

pronunciation.tip: Stress ES, EN and STINK. The k sound in "distinction" must be clear: "dih-STINK-shun."

nuance.usage_note: Formulated by Gregory Palamas in the fourteenth-century hesychast controversy and confirmed by councils in Constantinople. It explains how deification and the vision of the uncreated light are possible without confusing creature and Creator. It is a frequent topic in Orthodox-Catholic theological debate.

distinctions.note: Divine simplicity, central in Thomism, holds that God has no distinctions in being; critics think it conflicts with the essence-energies distinction.
The Trinity distinguishes persons; the essence-energies distinction distinguishes what God is from God acting.
Attributes are in Western thought only rationally distinct from God's essence.

collocations: the real distinction between essence and energies

examples.everyday: Our study group spent an hour on the essence-energies distinction and still had questions.
examples.professional: This seminar covers the essence-energies distinction in Palamas and its reception.
examples.analytical: The essence-energies distinction safeguards both divine transcendence and real participation.

nuance.etymology: Essence from Latin essentia (Greek ousia); energies from Greek energeia.
common_mistakes: Thinking it divides God into parts.
Writing it without the hyphen in formal contexts.

traditions.view: Dogmatic teaching, confirmed by the councils of Constantinople in the fourteenth century: God is unknowable in essence but truly present in His uncreated energies.
Traditional Thomist theology teaches divine simplicity and created grace; Catholic theologians today hold a range of views, some open to the distinction as compatible with Catholic teaching.
The distinction was not part of Reformation theology; most Protestants do not use it, though some recent theologians engage it in dialogue with Orthodoxy.

senses: Relating to Evagrius Ponticus, the fourth-century desert monk, or to his teaching on the passions, the eight thoughts, and pure prayer.

etymology: From Evagrius (Greek Euagrios) + the English suffix -an.

core.definition: Relating to Evagrius Ponticus, the fourth-century desert monk, or to his teaching on the passions, the eight thoughts, and pure prayer.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable, VAG, with the vowel of “bag”; the first syllable is a light “ih” or “eh.”

nuance.connotation: neutral; in patristic scholarship it can hint at the controversy over his Origenist speculation.
nuance.usage_note: An academic word found in books and lectures on early monasticism and Christian spirituality: “Evagrian spirituality,” “the Evagrian scheme of eight thoughts.” Scholars use it to trace his influence on later writers such as John Cassian, Maximus the Confessor and the Philokalia. It is rarely heard in ordinary parish talk.

distinctions.note: Origenist refers to the speculative theology of Origen and his followers; Evagrian names Evagrius's own system, which used Origenist ideas but is best known for its ascetic psychology.
Hesychast refers to the later Byzantine tradition of stillness and the Jesus Prayer, which drew on Evagrian teaching about prayer but is not the same thing.
Philokalic describes the whole anthology tradition of the Philokalia, in which Evagrian texts are only one strand.

examples.everyday: Our reading group noticed that the list of sins in that old prayer book is basically Evagrian.
examples.professional: This seminar traces the Evagrian scheme of the eight thoughts through Cassian to the medieval seven deadly sins.
examples.analytical: Maximus the Confessor adopts the Evagrian analysis of the passions while quietly correcting its Origenist cosmology.

nuance.etymology: From Evagrius (Greek Euagrios) + the English suffix -an.
common_mistakes: Writing it with a lowercase e; it comes from a proper name.
Stressing the first syllable as “EV-uh-gree-un.”

senses: Usually Evagrius Ponticus (died 399), a desert monk and teacher whose writings on the passions and prayer shaped all later Christian spirituality.

etymology: Greek Euagrios, from eu “well, good” + agra “hunting, catch”: roughly “good hunter.”

core.definition: Usually Evagrius Ponticus (died 399), a desert monk and teacher whose writings on the passions and prayer shaped all later Christian spirituality.

pronunciation.tip: Stress VAG, with the vowel of “bag”; the ending is a soft “ee-us.”

nuance.connotation: neutral; admired as a master of the spiritual life, yet linked with condemned Origenist ideas.
nuance.usage_note: In theology and church history, “Evagrius” alone almost always means Evagrius Ponticus. Context matters, because Evagrius Scholasticus (sixth century) was a different person, a church historian. Scholars often say “Evagrius” in lectures after first giving the full name.

distinctions.note: Evagrius Scholasticus was a sixth-century church historian from Syria, not the desert monk.
Cassian carried Evagrius's teaching on the eight thoughts to the Latin West, usually without naming him.
Macarius of Egypt was a leading desert elder and one of Evagrius's teachers, not his follower.

examples.everyday: Our priest quoted Evagrius tonight: he said that the monk who prays truly is a theologian.
examples.professional: Students should read Evagrius's Praktikos before turning to the chapters on prayer.
examples.analytical: Evagrius moves the battle against sin inward, from outward acts to the thoughts that first suggest them.

nuance.etymology: Greek Euagrios, from eu “well, good” + agra “hunting, catch”: roughly “good hunter.”
common_mistakes: Confusing him with Evagrius Scholasticus, the church historian.
Pronouncing it “EV-uh-gree-us” with first-syllable stress.

senses: A fourth-century monk from Pontus (died 399) who lived in the Egyptian desert and systematized the eight evil thoughts and the theology of pure prayer.

etymology: Greek Euagrios ho Pontikos, “Evagrius from Pontus,” the region on the Black Sea coast of Asia Minor where he was born.

core.definition: A fourth-century monk from Pontus (died 399) who lived in the Egyptian desert and systematized the eight evil thoughts and the theology of pure prayer.

pronunciation.tip: Two stresses: VAG in the first name and PAHN in the second. Ponticus has a hard c, like “k.”

nuance.connotation: neutral; highly respected for his ascetic teaching, though his speculative Origenist ideas were later condemned.
nuance.usage_note: Ordained a deacon by Gregory the Theologian, Evagrius went to Jerusalem and then to the monastic deserts of Nitria and Kellia, where he learned from Macarius the Great. His Praktikos, On Prayer and other works teach the eight thoughts (gluttony, lust, avarice, sadness, anger, acedia, vainglory and pride), dispassion, and imageless pure prayer. Some of his works survived under other names, including On Prayer under the name of Nilus; through Cassian his list became the Western seven deadly sins.

distinctions.note: Origen was a third-century Alexandrian theologian whose speculative cosmology Evagrius took over and developed.
John Climacus wrote The Ladder about two centuries later and used many Evagrian categories within a less speculative framework.
A sixth-century church historian, unrelated to the desert monk.

collocations: Evagrius Ponticus on the eight thoughts

examples.everyday: If you liked the Ladder, try Evagrius Ponticus; he wrote much earlier about the same struggle with thoughts.
examples.professional: Evagrius Ponticus offers the first systematic map of the passions in Christian monastic literature.
examples.analytical: For Evagrius Ponticus, prayer is the mind laying aside every concept so that it can stand before God without images.

nuance.analogy: The desert's first psychologist: he catalogued temptations the way a doctor catalogues symptoms.
nuance.etymology: Greek Euagrios ho Pontikos, “Evagrius from Pontus,” the region on the Black Sea coast of Asia Minor where he was born.
common_mistakes: Saying “Pon-TEE-kus”; the stress is on the first syllable of Ponticus.
Treating him as a heretic without qualification; his practical teaching was received by the Church even though his speculative ideas were condemned.

senses: In Orthodox spirituality, the continual, heartfelt remembrance of God through the day, often kept by the Jesus Prayer.

etymology: English rendering of Greek mnēmē Theou, “memory of God,” with “ever” for its unceasing character.

core.definition: In Orthodox spirituality, the continual, heartfelt remembrance of God through the day, often kept by the Jesus Prayer.

pronunciation.tip: Stress EV and MEM and GOD; “of” is reduced to a quick “uv.” In “memory” the middle vowel is very light: MEM-uh-ree or even MEM-ree.

nuance.connotation: positive; it names a goal of the whole Christian life.
nuance.usage_note: A translation term found in English versions of Orthodox spiritual writers; more common equivalents are “remembrance of God” and “unceasing remembrance of God” (Greek mnēmē Theou). It appears in spiritual reading, retreats and talks on prayer. Do not confuse it with “Memory eternal,” the hymn sung for the departed.

distinctions.note: “Memory eternal” is a prayer that God remember the departed; ever-memory of God is our remembering of God.
Unceasing prayer is the practice; ever-memory of God is the inner state that practice builds.
Remembrance of death keeps one's own mortality in view, while ever-memory of God keeps God himself in view.

collocations: the ever-memory of God in the heart
grow in the ever-memory of God
the Jesus Prayer and the ever-memory of God

examples.everyday: My spiritual father says the ever-memory of God starts small: a short prayer when the alarm goes off, at lunch and in traffic.
examples.professional: In tonight's retreat talk I want to show how the fathers connect the ever-memory of God with the guarding of the heart.
examples.analytical: The ever-memory of God is not an act of recollection added to other thoughts but a stable orientation of the whole person toward God.

nuance.analogy: Like a mother who is always aware of her sleeping baby, whatever else she is doing.
nuance.etymology: English rendering of Greek mnēmē Theou, “memory of God,” with “ever” for its unceasing character.
common_mistakes: Confusing it with “Memory eternal” at funerals.
Thinking it means thinking about God intellectually; the fathers mean an attentive, prayerful awareness of the heart.
nuance.biblical_note: The idea draws on Paul's call in 1 Thessalonians 5:17 to pray constantly, and on Psalm 16:8, where the psalmist says he keeps the Lord always before him and so will not be moved.

senses: In Orthodox monastic practice, the regular disclosure of one's thoughts and temptations to a spiritual father or mother.

etymology: Greek exagoreusis, from exagoreuein “to declare openly,” from ex “out” + agoreuein “to speak in public.”

core.definition: In Orthodox monastic practice, the regular disclosure of one's thoughts and temptations to a spiritual father or mother.

pronunciation.tip: The usual English stress is on ROO; Greek speakers say ek-sah-GHO-ref-sis, so expect variation.

nuance.connotation: positive; associated with humility, openness and spiritual healing.
nuance.usage_note: A technical term in studies of desert monasticism and spiritual direction, often translated “disclosure of thoughts” or “manifestation of thoughts.” It differs from sacramental confession: the elder may be a monk who is not a priest, and the aim is discernment and guidance rather than absolution. American Orthodox lay people usually just say “telling your thoughts to your spiritual father.”

distinctions.note: Sacramental confession is a mystery of the Church with a priest's prayer of absolution; exagoreusis is the ongoing revealing of thoughts to an elder for guidance.
Exomologesis is the general Greek term for confession, of sins or of faith; exagoreusis is specifically the opening of one's thoughts.
Spiritual direction is the broad Western term for guidance; exagoreusis names the disciple's act of disclosure within it.

examples.everyday: The nun told us that exagoreusis isn't confession; she simply tells the abbess each evening what thoughts troubled her.
examples.professional: In my chapter I argue that exagoreusis was central to the formation of novices in the Egyptian desert.
examples.analytical: Exagoreusis presupposes that a thought loses its power once it is brought into the light and shared with an experienced elder.

nuance.analogy: Like opening a window in a stuffy room: what is brought into the light loses its hold.
nuance.etymology: Greek exagoreusis, from exagoreuein “to declare openly,” from ex “out” + agoreuein “to speak in public.”
common_mistakes: Treating it as a synonym for sacramental confession.
Spelling it “exagoresis”; the Greek has -eusis.

senses: The three central Christian virtues named by Paul; in The Ladder of Divine Ascent, the summit of the spiritual life.

etymology: English renderings of Greek pistis, elpis and agapē.

core.definition: The three central Christian virtues named by Paul; in The Ladder of Divine Ascent, the summit of the spiritual life.

pronunciation.tip: Give each noun a stress and reduce “and” to “un.” The th in “faith” is voiceless; don't turn it into “s” or “t.”

nuance.usage_note: Americans know the phrase from 1 Corinthians 13, read at countless weddings, often in older translations as “faith, hope, and charity.” In Orthodox spiritual reading it refers to the thirtieth and last step of Saint John Climacus's Ladder, “on faith, hope and love.” Catholic catechesis calls them the theological virtues.

distinctions.note: Theological virtues is the scholastic and Catholic term for the same three, distinguished from the four cardinal virtues.
“Charity” is the older translation of agapē; modern American readers hear “charity” as giving to the poor, so “love” is clearer.
The cardinal virtues are prudence, justice, courage and temperance, the natural moral virtues.

collocations: the greatest of these is love
grow in faith, hope, and love
the virtues of faith, hope, and love

examples.everyday: We had “faith, hope, and love” engraved inside our wedding rings.
examples.professional: Climacus ends his Ladder not with a technique but with faith, hope, and love, and so will this course.
examples.analytical: In the Ladder, faith, hope, and love form the summit because every earlier step was a preparation for love, which alone remains.

nuance.analogy: Three strands of one rope, with love as the strand that holds the others.
nuance.etymology: English renderings of Greek pistis, elpis and agapē.
common_mistakes: Leaving out “and” or the comma before it in formal writing.
Thinking “charity” in older Bibles means donations.
nuance.biblical_note: In 1 Corinthians 13:13 Paul concludes his hymn to love by saying that faith, hope and love abide, these three, but the greatest of these is love (Greek pistis, elpis, agapē). He links the same triad in 1 Thessalonians 1:3 and 5:8, where faith and love are a breastplate and the hope of salvation a helmet.

senses: In the Orthodox calendar, a week in which the usual Wednesday and Friday fast is lifted, such as Bright Week after Pascha.

etymology: English compound of “fast” (Old English fæstan, to abstain) and “free.”

core.definition: In the Orthodox calendar, a week in which the usual Wednesday and Friday fast is lifted, such as Bright Week after Pascha.

pronunciation.tip: Stress FAST and WEEK; “free” is lighter. Americans say “fast” with the vowel of “cat.”

nuance.connotation: positive; associated with feasting and joy.
nuance.usage_note: Orthodox parish calendars mark these weeks so people know they may eat freely on Wednesday and Friday. They are usually the period from Nativity to the eve of Theophany, the week after the Sunday of the Publican and the Pharisee, Bright Week, and the week after Pentecost. Cheesefare week is sometimes listed too, but meat is already given up then, so it is only partly free.

distinctions.note: Bright Week is the most famous fast-free week, the week after Pascha, but not the only one.
In Cheesefare week dairy is allowed every day but meat is not, so it is not fully fast-free.
A feast day is one day; a fast-free week is a whole week without the weekly fast.

examples.everyday: It's a fast-free week, so let's have the coffee hour with cheese and sausage on Wednesday.
examples.professional: Please note in the parish bulletin that next week is fast-free, following the Sunday of the Publican and the Pharisee.
examples.analytical: The fast-free week after the Publican and the Pharisee warns against the Pharisee's boast that he fasts twice a week.

nuance.etymology: English compound of “fast” (Old English fæstan, to abstain) and “free.”
common_mistakes: Assuming no Communion preparation is needed; the fast before Communion still applies.
Writing it without the hyphen as “fast free week.”

senses: The Church's rule for which foods may be eaten on which days and seasons, applied to each person with a priest's guidance.

etymology: English “fasting” (from Old English fæstan, to hold firm, abstain) + “rule” (Latin regula).

core.definition: The Church's rule for which foods may be eaten on which days and seasons, applied to each person with a priest's guidance.

pronunciation.tip: Stress FAST; the t is pronounced, not dropped, and “rule” rhymes with “cool.”

nuance.connotation: neutral; seen as discipline that serves freedom, not legalism.
nuance.usage_note: Orthodox Christians talk about “keeping the fasting rule” or asking their priest about “my fasting rule.” The full rule covers Wednesdays and Fridays, the four fasting seasons (Great Lent, the Apostles' Fast, the Dormition Fast and the Nativity Fast) and some single days such as September 14 and August 29. On strict days it excludes meat, dairy, eggs, fish, wine and oil, with relaxations on weekends and some feasts. Priests often adapt it for health, pregnancy, work and family life.

distinctions.note: In Catholic usage abstinence means giving up meat; fasting means eating less. The Orthodox fasting rule mainly concerns kinds of food.
A prayer rule fixes one's daily prayers; a fasting rule fixes one's eating.
The Eucharistic fast is abstaining from all food and drink before Communion, separate from the calendar fasts.

collocations: ask your priest about your fasting rule

examples.everyday: Since the baby came, Father told me to keep a lighter fasting rule this Lent.
examples.professional: Pastorally, the fasting rule should be presented as an ideal applied with discernment, not a test of who is most Orthodox.
examples.analytical: The fasting rule disciplines desire collectively: the whole Church fasts together, so personal effort is held within a common rhythm.

nuance.analogy: Like a training plan from a coach: the same goal for the team, adjusted for each athlete.
nuance.etymology: English “fasting” (from Old English fæstan, to hold firm, abstain) + “rule” (Latin regula).
common_mistakes: Thinking the rule is the same for everyone regardless of health or circumstances.
Treating fish as always allowed; on strict fast days it is not.

traditions.view: The fasting rule is mainly abstention from certain foods (meat, dairy, eggs, fish, wine and oil) on Wednesdays, Fridays and in four fasting seasons, plus fasting from all food before Communion, adjusted by one's priest.

Current Latin rules require fasting (one full meal and two smaller ones) on Ash Wednesday and Good Friday and abstinence from meat on Fridays of Lent in the United States, plus a one-hour fast before Communion; Eastern Catholic churches keep their own, often stricter, rules.

Most Protestant churches have no binding fasting rule; fasting is voluntary and personal, often for prayer and discernment. Some Anglicans and Lutherans encourage Lenten fasting, and many evangelicals and Pentecostals practice periods of total fasting.

senses: Fr. Georges Florovsky (1893-1979), Russian Orthodox priest and historian who called for a “neopatristic synthesis,” a return to the Church Fathers.

etymology: Russian surname Florovsky (Флоровский).

core.definition: Fr. Georges Florovsky (1893-1979), Russian Orthodox priest and historian who called for a “neopatristic synthesis,” a return to the Church Fathers.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable, RAHF; the v sounds like f before the s. In Russian it is flah-ROF-skee.

nuance.connotation: neutral; widely respected as a founder of modern Orthodox theology.
nuance.usage_note: Born in Odessa, Florovsky taught at the Saint Sergius Institute in Paris, served as dean of Saint Vladimir's Seminary in New York, and later taught at Harvard and Princeton. His Ways of Russian Theology criticized Western influence on Russian theology and urged a recovery of the patristic mind. He was also a leading Orthodox voice in the early World Council of Churches. Students cite him simply as “Florovsky.”

distinctions.note: Sergius Bulgakov, his colleague in Paris, developed a sophiology that Florovsky's patristic approach opposed.
Vladimir Lossky shared the neopatristic program but stressed apophatic theology and the Holy Spirit.
Alexander Schmemann, his successor as dean at Saint Vladimir's, focused on liturgical theology.

collocations: Ways of Russian Theology by Florovsky

examples.everyday: Our priest studied at Saint Vladimir's, so he quotes Florovsky all the time about “the mind of the Fathers.”
examples.professional: For the comprehensive exam, be ready to compare Florovsky's neopatristic synthesis with Bulgakov's sophiology.
examples.analytical: Florovsky's call to return to the Fathers was not antiquarian; he wanted their mind, not merely their words.

nuance.etymology: Russian surname Florovsky (Флоровский).
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable as “FLOR-ov-skee.”
Confusing his neopatristic synthesis with a simple repetition of old texts.

senses: The rare ascetic calling of holy fools, who deliberately appear mad or absurd to hide their holiness and expose worldly pride.

etymology: English rendering of Greek mōria dia Christon, from Paul's phrase “fools for Christ's sake” (1 Corinthians 4:10).

core.definition: The rare ascetic calling of holy fools, who deliberately appear mad or absurd to hide their holiness and expose worldly pride.

pronunciation.tip: Stress FOOL and CHRIST; “for” is reduced to “fer.” Christ rhymes with “iced.”

nuance.connotation: positive in hagiography, though the behavior itself shocks and offends.
nuance.usage_note: The Greek term is salos and the Russian yurodstvo; a holy fool is a fool-for-Christ (Russian yurodivy). Famous examples include Symeon of Emesa, Andrew of Constantinople, Basil the Blessed of Moscow and Xenia of Saint Petersburg. Orthodox writers stress that it is an exceptional calling that should not be imitated without a clear blessing; in everyday speech people sometimes use the phrase loosely for any unpopular Christian stand.

distinctions.note: Holy folly is a near-synonym used especially in scholarship.
Eccentricity is harmless oddness; foolishness for Christ is a deliberate ascetic path aimed at humility.
Paul's phrase refers to how the gospel looks to the world, the basis on which the holy fool's calling rests.

collocations: the path of foolishness for Christ
the podvig of foolishness for Christ
saints who practiced foolishness for Christ

examples.everyday: Saint Xenia gave away everything and wore her late husband's clothes; that's what foolishness for Christ looked like for her.
examples.professional: Hagiographers present foolishness for Christ as a prophetic critique of a society that had grown comfortable with Christianity.
examples.analytical: Foolishness for Christ radicalizes humility: the saint accepts contempt in order to destroy the very possibility of vainglory.

nuance.analogy: Like a king dressing as a beggar so that people see the city's true heart.
nuance.etymology: English rendering of Greek mōria dia Christon, from Paul's phrase “fools for Christ's sake” (1 Corinthians 4:10).
common_mistakes: Using it of mental illness; the tradition distinguishes deliberate folly from real madness.
Saying “foolness”; the noun is foolishness.
nuance.biblical_note: In 1 Corinthians 4:10 Paul says the apostles are fools for Christ's sake while the Corinthians think themselves wise. In 1 Corinthians 1:18-25 he calls the word of the cross folly to those who are perishing and says God's foolishness is wiser than men. Greek mōros, “foolish,” is the root.

senses: Gluttony, literally “madness of the belly”: the first of the eight evil thoughts in Evagrius and the desert fathers.

etymology: Greek gastrimargia, from gastēr “belly” + margos “raging, mad, greedy.”

core.definition: Gluttony, literally “madness of the belly”: the first of the eight evil thoughts in Evagrius and the desert fathers.

pronunciation.tip: In English the stress usually falls on MAHR; in Greek it is gas-tree-mar-YEE-ah. The g in -gia is soft in English.

nuance.usage_note: A Greek technical term met in translations of Evagrius, Cassian and the Philokalia, and in courses on the passions; ordinary speakers say “gluttony.” The fathers treat it as more than overeating: it includes eating too early, too eagerly, too delicately or with too much attention to food. Step 14 of The Ladder of Divine Ascent is devoted to it.

distinctions.note: Gluttony is the ordinary English word; gastrimargia is the Greek technical term with its ascetic analysis.
Acedia is spiritual listlessness; gastrimargia is disordered desire for food.
Porneia (lust) is the next thought on Evagrius's list, which the fathers say gluttony feeds.

examples.everyday: Father joked that checking the coffee-hour table during the Gospel was a mild case of gastrimargia.
examples.professional: Evagrius places gastrimargia first because the body's most basic appetite opens the door to the others.
examples.analytical: Gastrimargia is defined less by quantity than by attachment: the mind becomes captive to the pleasure of the stomach.

nuance.etymology: Greek gastrimargia, from gastēr “belly” + margos “raging, mad, greedy.”
common_mistakes: Treating it only as eating too much; the fathers include eating too eagerly or delicately.
Pronouncing the g in -gia as hard in English.

senses: In Orthodox monasticism, an elder: an experienced monk who guides disciples spiritually, the Greek equivalent of the Russian starets.

etymology: Greek gerōn “old man, elder” (compare gerontology).

core.definition: In Orthodox monasticism, an elder: an experienced monk who guides disciples spiritually, the Greek equivalent of the Russian starets.

pronunciation.tip: American Orthodox speakers usually follow the Greek: the g sounds like y and the stress is on the first syllable. Some English speakers say “GEH-rahn.”

nuance.connotation: positive; implies holiness, experience and spiritual authority, not just old age.
nuance.usage_note: Used in writings about Mount Athos, desert spirituality and modern Greek elders such as Saint Paisios and Saint Porphyrios. The plural is gerontes. When speaking to an elder, Greeks use the form “Geronta.” An elder need not be a priest or old in years; what matters is spiritual experience and the gift of discernment.

distinctions.note: Starets is the Russian word for the same figure; geron is the Greek.
Abba, “father,” was the title for desert elders in Egypt and Syria.
A spiritual father may be any confessor; a geron suggests a recognized charismatic elder.
A hegumen is the administrative head of a monastery, who may or may not be an elder.

examples.everyday: When we visited Athos, the monks said their geron would see pilgrims after Vespers.
examples.professional: In the Gerontikon the geron rarely lectures; he answers a disciple's question with a short word or an action.
examples.analytical: The authority of the geron is charismatic rather than institutional, grounded in a life that others recognize as transformed.

nuance.analogy: A mountain guide who has walked the path many times and knows where the cliffs are.
nuance.etymology: Greek gerōn “old man, elder” (compare gerontology).
common_mistakes: Assuming any old monk is a geron; the title implies spiritual gifts.
Pronouncing the g hard in Orthodox settings, where the Greek “y” sound is expected.

senses: The Greek form used to address or speak about an elder (“Geronta”), as Greek and Greek-American Orthodox call a spiritual father.

etymology: Modern Greek Geronta, the vocative and accusative of gerōn “elder.”

core.definition: The Greek form used to address or speak about an elder (“Geronta”), as Greek and Greek-American Orthodox call a spiritual father.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable; the Greek nt is said like “nd,” and the g like y.

nuance.usage_note: Grammatically it is the vocative and accusative of geron, and in modern Greek speech it serves as a title: “Geronta, bless.” Greek-American Orthodox, especially those close to Athonite monasteries in the United States, use it when greeting or speaking about their elder. In English writing it often appears as “Geronta Ephraim” or “our Geronta.”

distinctions.note: Geron is the dictionary form; geronta is the form used in direct address and as a title.
“Father” is the ordinary English address for any priest; Geronta is reserved for a recognized elder or abbot.
Gerontissa is the feminine counterpart, used for an abbess or spiritual mother.

examples.everyday: We drove up to the monastery on Saturday and Geronta gave us a few minutes after the Liturgy.
examples.professional: Pilgrims address the abbot as Geronta, which signals spiritual fatherhood rather than administrative rank.
examples.analytical: The use of “Geronta” in American Athonite communities shows how Greek monastic forms of address have been transplanted into an English-speaking setting.

nuance.etymology: Modern Greek Geronta, the vocative and accusative of gerōn “elder.”
common_mistakes: Saying “Gerontas” when addressing him; the address form is Geronta.
Using it for a married parish priest; it normally refers to a monastic elder.

senses: A Greek collection of the sayings and stories of the desert fathers and mothers, known in English as the Sayings of the Desert Fathers.

etymology: Greek gerontikon (biblion), “book of the elders,” from gerōn “elder.”

core.definition: A Greek collection of the sayings and stories of the desert fathers and mothers, known in English as the Sayings of the Desert Fathers.

pronunciation.tip: Following Greek, stress the last syllable; English speakers also say “geh-RAHN-tih-kahn.”

nuance.connotation: positive; a classic of spiritual reading.
nuance.usage_note: Scholars usually call the collections Apophthegmata Patrum (Latin, “sayings of the fathers”); in Greek monastic use the book is the Gerontikon, and in Slavonic the Paterik. The best-known form is the Alphabetical Collection, arranged by the names of the elders, from Abba Antony onward; there is also a Systematic Collection arranged by topics. In English it is often read in translations such as The Sayings of the Desert Fathers.

distinctions.note: The scholarly title for the same body of sayings, in its various collections.
The Slavonic name for similar collections, including later Russian ones such as the Kiev Caves Paterik.
The Philokalia is an eighteenth-century anthology of longer treatises on prayer, not short sayings.
Palladius's Lausiac History is a narrative of monks' lives, not a sayings collection.

examples.everyday: Before bed I read one story from the Gerontikon; they're short, but they stay with me all day.
examples.professional: This week we'll compare the Alphabetical and Systematic collections of the Gerontikon.
examples.analytical: The Gerontikon teaches less by doctrine than by encounter: a single word from an elder exposes the disciple's heart.

nuance.analogy: A family album of the desert, in which each snapshot holds a lesson.
nuance.etymology: Greek gerontikon (biblion), “book of the elders,” from gerōn “elder.”
common_mistakes: Thinking it is a single book written by one author; it is a compilation that grew over time.
Confusing it with the Philokalia.

senses: In Greek Orthodox use, an abbess or a female spiritual elder, the feminine of geron; used both as a title and in address.

etymology: Greek gerontissa, the feminine of gerōn “elder.”

core.definition: In Greek Orthodox use, an abbess or a female spiritual elder, the feminine of geron; used both as a title and in address.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable, RAWN; the g sounds like y and the nt like “nd,” following Greek.

nuance.usage_note: Nuns, pilgrims and Greek-American Orthodox call the abbess of a women's monastery “Gerontissa,” often before her name (Gerontissa Markella). It suggests spiritual motherhood, not just leadership. In Slavic usage the abbess is called igumenia or matushka.

distinctions.note: Abbess is the general English title for a convent's head; Gerontissa carries the added sense of a spiritual mother.
Amma, “mother,” was the title of the early desert mothers in Egypt.
Hegumenia (Slavonic igumenia) is the formal title of the abbess's office.

examples.everyday: We should ask Gerontissa's blessing before we take pictures in the monastery church.
examples.professional: The Gerontissa assigns each sister's obedience and hears the nuns' thoughts.
examples.analytical: The figure of the Gerontissa shows that charismatic spiritual eldership in the Orthodox tradition is not limited to men.

nuance.etymology: Greek gerontissa, the feminine of gerōn “elder.”
common_mistakes: Calling her “Mother Geronta”; the feminine form is Gerontissa.
Pronouncing the first g hard.

senses: A grace of heartfelt weeping, out of sorrow for sin or out of love for God, valued in Orthodox spirituality as a sign of repentance.

etymology: English phrase translating Latin donum lacrimarum and Greek charisma tōn dakryōn.

core.definition: A grace of heartfelt weeping, out of sorrow for sin or out of love for God, valued in Orthodox spirituality as a sign of repentance.

pronunciation.tip: Stress GIFT and TEARS; “of” reduces to “uv.” Tears rhymes with “years,” not with “cares.”

nuance.connotation: positive; it is considered a gift of grace, not emotional weakness.
nuance.usage_note: Found in spiritual reading and talks on prayer, often connected with penthos (mourning) and katanyxis (compunction). Writers such as John Climacus, Isaac the Syrian and Symeon the New Theologian speak of tears that cleanse the soul and even renew baptism. Spiritual fathers warn against forcing tears or taking pride in them; they are received, not produced.

distinctions.note: Penthos is the joyful mourning of the heart; the gift of tears is its outward sign.
Compunction (katanyxis) is the piercing of the heart that often brings tears, but it can exist without them.
Sentimentality is easy emotional crying about oneself; the gift of tears is focused on God and leads to change.

collocations: pray for the gift of tears
the gift of tears and compunction
the gift of tears in prayer

examples.everyday: My godmother says she prays for the gift of tears, because she feels her prayers have become dry.
examples.professional: Climacus treats the gift of tears in his step on mourning, warning that tears can be either from God or from vanity.
examples.analytical: The gift of tears signals that repentance has reached the heart, where knowledge of sin becomes grief and then consolation.

nuance.analogy: Like spring rain softening hard ground so that seed can grow.
nuance.etymology: English phrase translating Latin donum lacrimarum and Greek charisma tōn dakryōn.
common_mistakes: Thinking it means ordinary emotional crying.
Pronouncing “tears” like the verb “tear” (rip).
nuance.biblical_note: The tradition draws on Matthew 5:4, where Jesus calls those who mourn blessed, for they shall be comforted; on Luke 7:38, where the sinful woman weeps at Jesus' feet; and on Peter's bitter weeping after his denial in Luke 22:62.

senses: The condition of a human being, body and soul, filled with God's glory, as in the risen Christ and the saints at the resurrection.

etymology: English “glorified” (from Latin glorificare, to make glorious) + “state.”

core.definition: The condition of a human being, body and soul, filled with God's glory, as in the risen Christ and the saints at the resurrection.

pronunciation.tip: Stress GLOR and STATE; -fied sounds like “fyed,” one syllable.

nuance.usage_note: A term of theological writing, found in Orthodox, Catholic and Protestant discussions of the resurrection body and deification. Orthodox writers link it to the uncreated light seen at the Transfiguration and to the radiance of saints in this life as a foretaste. It is rare in ordinary conversation, where people say “in glory” or “in heaven.”

distinctions.note: Glorification is the process or act of being glorified; in Orthodox usage it also means the formal recognition of a saint.
Theosis is the whole path of union with God; the glorified state is its fulfillment.
The intermediate state is the condition of souls between death and the resurrection, before final glorification.

collocations: the glorified state of the body
the glorified state of the saints

examples.everyday: In our study group someone asked whether we'll recognize each other in the glorified state; our priest said yes, as the disciples recognized the risen Lord.
examples.professional: The Transfiguration offers the disciples a glimpse of Christ's glorified state before the Passion.
examples.analytical: The glorified state is not an escape from the body but the body's transfiguration, freed from corruption while remaining truly human.

nuance.analogy: Like iron in a fire: still iron, but glowing with the fire's heat and light.
nuance.etymology: English “glorified” (from Latin glorificare, to make glorious) + “state.”
common_mistakes: Assuming it means a purely spiritual existence without a body.
Saying “glorify state”; use the past participle “glorified.”
nuance.biblical_note: Paul says in 1 Corinthians 15:42-44 that the body is sown perishable and raised imperishable, sown a physical body and raised a spiritual body. Philippians 3:21 says Christ will change our lowly body to be like his glorious body, and Romans 8:30 lists glorification as the end of God's saving work. The Greek root is doxa, “glory.”

senses: In Maximus the Confessor, the personal, deliberating will of fallen humans who hesitate between options, as opposed to the natural will.

etymology: Greek gnōmikos, from gnōmē “judgment, opinion, inclination,” from gignōskein “to know.”

core.definition: In Maximus the Confessor, the personal, deliberating will of fallen humans who hesitate between options, as opposed to the natural will.

pronunciation.tip: The g is silent: say “NOH-mik.” Stress the first syllable.

nuance.connotation: neutral; in Maximus it suggests the hesitation and uncertainty of fallen choice.
nuance.usage_note: A term of patristic and dogmatic theology, from Greek thelēma gnōmikon; gnōmē means a settled disposition or opinion formed by deliberation. Maximus distinguished it from the natural will (thelēma physikon) and, in his mature thought, denied that Christ had a gnomic will, since he does not deliberate in ignorance or doubt. The term appears in discussions of the Monothelete controversy and of human freedom.

distinctions.note: The natural will is the God-given capacity of a nature to desire its good; the gnomic will is a person's deliberating mode of willing.
Free will is the general concept; for Maximus true freedom is the natural will moving toward God without the wavering of gnome.
In grammar and literature “gnomic” means proverb-like (“gnomic aorist”), a different use of the same Greek root.

examples.everyday: Our professor explained gnomic will this way: it's the part of us that keeps going back and forth about what's good.
examples.professional: In the Disputation with Pyrrhus, Maximus argues that the Lord's human will was natural, not gnomic.
examples.analytical: Deification heals the gnomic will so that personal choice comes to rest in the natural will's movement toward God.

nuance.analogy: A traveler checking the map at every fork; a saint walks home without needing to ask the way.
nuance.etymology: Greek gnōmikos, from gnōmē “judgment, opinion, inclination,” from gignōskein “to know.”
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the g: it is silent, as in “gnome.”
Thinking Maximus denies Christ had a human will; he denies only the gnomic mode of willing.

senses: A title of Jesus Christ as one divine person who is both fully God and fully human (Greek Theanthropos).

etymology: English calque of Greek theanthrōpos, from theos “God” + anthrōpos “human being.”

core.definition: A title of Jesus Christ as one divine person who is both fully God and fully human (Greek Theanthropos).

pronunciation.tip: Stress GOD, with the vowel of “father”; “man” has a lighter secondary stress.

nuance.usage_note: Used in Orthodox preaching and theology, often translating Greek Theanthropos or Russian Bogochelovek; Orthodox writers like to call Christ “the God-man” and the Church “the God-man's body.” Russian thinkers such as Vladimir Soloviev spoke of “Godmanhood.” Capitalize “God” and use the hyphen.

distinctions.note: A demigod is half divine and half human in myth; the God-man is wholly God and wholly human.
Incarnate Word stresses the eternal Son taking flesh; God-man stresses the result, one person in two natures.
Theandric is the adjective for Christ's divine-human actions, as in “theandric energy.”

examples.everyday: Father said we pray to Christ as the God-man, not as a good teacher or a superhero.
examples.professional: Chalcedon teaches that the God-man is one person in two natures, without confusion and without separation.
examples.analytical: Because the God-man unites divinity and humanity in himself, human nature is opened to deification in him.

nuance.etymology: English calque of Greek theanthrōpos, from theos “God” + anthrōpos “human being.”
common_mistakes: Writing “god-man” in lowercase in Christian contexts.
Understanding it as a man who became a god; it means God who became man.

senses: Sorrow for sin that comes from God and leads to repentance and salvation, unlike worldly grief, which leads to despair.

etymology: From the King James rendering of Greek hē kata theon lypē, “grief according to God.”

core.definition: Sorrow for sin that comes from God and leads to repentance and salvation, unlike worldly grief, which leads to despair.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable of each word; the d in “godly” is light, almost swallowed. Sorrow is said “SAHR-oh” by most Americans.

nuance.connotation: positive; healthy and hopeful, not depressive.
nuance.usage_note: A phrase from 2 Corinthians 7:10 in older translations, widely used in sermons and Bible studies; the RSV renders it “godly grief.” Orthodox spiritual writers connect it with joyful mourning (penthos) and contrast it with the passion of sadness (lypē) and with despair. It sounds churchy in everyday speech.

distinctions.note: Worldly grief is regret centered on loss or shame and, Paul says, produces death.
Remorse is painful regret, which may or may not turn toward God.
Penthos is the ascetic term for lasting, joyful mourning, close to godly sorrow but a more developed state.

examples.everyday: In Bible study we talked about the difference between godly sorrow and just feeling bad about getting caught.
examples.professional: This sermon contrasts Peter's godly sorrow, which led him back to Christ, with Judas's despair.
examples.analytical: Godly sorrow differs from worldly grief not in intensity but in direction: it turns toward God's mercy rather than inward.

nuance.analogy: Like a fever that breaks and leads to healing, rather than one that weakens the body.
nuance.etymology: From the King James rendering of Greek hē kata theon lypē, “grief according to God.”
common_mistakes: Thinking “godly” means “very great”; it means “according to God.”
Equating it with chronic guilt or depression.
nuance.biblical_note: In 2 Corinthians 7:8-11 Paul says his severe letter grieved the Corinthians, but in a godly way. He explains in 7:10 that godly grief (Greek kata theon lypē) produces a repentance that leads to salvation and brings no regret, while worldly grief produces death. The RSV says “godly grief.”

senses: The forty-day Orthodox fasting season of repentance before Holy Week and Pascha, beginning on Clean Monday.

etymology: English “Lent,” from Old English lencten “spring,” with “great” translating Greek megalē.
